solutions.name: dot_loop
solutions.headline: the definition as an algorithm
solutions.mechanism: Walk both lists together, multiply each pair, accumulate. The length check matters because the operation is undefined for mismatched lengths — there is no sensible answer, so failing loudly beats guessing.
solutions.why: The accumulator starts at 0.0 rather than 0 so the return type is a float even for integer inputs. Indexing with range(len(a)) is the one place in this lesson where an index is genuinely needed — you are walking two lists in step.

solutions.name: dot_numpy
solutions.headline: the same result, loop pushed into C
solutions.mechanism: np.dot and np.matmul (also spelled @) agree for 1-D inputs and diverge only in higher dimensions: np.dot sums over the last axis of one and the second-to-last of the other, while matmul broadcasts stacks of matrices. For two vectors, either is right.
solutions.code:
def dot_numpy(a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.dot(a, b))
solutions.why: The float() matters more than it looks: without it you return np.float64, which behaves almost like a Python float right up until it does not — it will not JSON-serialise, and it leaks numpy semantics into code that expected a plain number.

solutions.name: magnitude_loop
solutions.headline: Pythagoras, nothing more
solutions.mechanism: The length of [3, 4] is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 3 and 4. Squaring removes signs so direction cannot cancel length out; the root brings the answer back to the original units.
solutions.why: A comprehension plus sum() is idiomatic Python and allowed here — exercise 1 already proved you can accumulate by hand, and the point of this one is Pythagoras. Using a generator, sum(x ** 2 for x in v), is marginally better for very long inputs since it never materialises the intermediate list.

solutions.name: magnitude
solutions.headline: the same sum, vectorised
solutions.mechanism: square, sum, sqrt — composed into a single expression. Nothing about this changes when the vector has 4096 components instead of two, which is why two-dimensional intuition is worth building.
solutions.code:
def magnitude(v: np.ndarray) -> float:
    return float(np.sqrt(np.sum(np.square(v))))
solutions.why: np.linalg.norm(v) does the same job in one call and is what you would reach for in real code. Write it out at least once, though — seeing square, sum and sqrt compose is where the vectorised style starts to feel natural. Neither version survives extreme inputs: both overflow to inf around 1e200, because both square before summing.
solutions.trap: Both versions overflow to inf around 1e200 — squaring before summing is the reason.

solutions.name: normalise
solutions.headline: keep the direction, throw away the length
solutions.mechanism: Dividing a vector by its own magnitude leaves it pointing exactly where it was, with length precisely 1. Every such vector lands on the unit circle. The zero vector is the one case with no answer: no direction to preserve, and the division would be by zero.
solutions.why: Calling magnitude(v) rather than rewriting the formula gives you one source of truth. Naming the local `length` and not `magnitude` matters — a local of the same name shadows the function, and the next person to add a second call inside this function gets a confusing TypeError.

solutions.name: cosine_similarity
solutions.headline: why the division works
solutions.mechanism: One identity sits underneath the whole exercise: a · b = |a| × |b| × cos θ. The dot product was never purely about agreement — it is agreement scaled by both lengths. Divide both sides by |a| × |b| and the lengths cancel, leaving the angle alone. You are not inventing a metric; you are rearranging an identity to isolate what you actually wanted.
solutions.why: np.dot(normalise(a), normalise(b)) is equally correct and returns the identical value bit for bit — shorter, and it inherits the zero-vector check from normalise for free. The version above was chosen only because it mirrors the formula in the docstring. The zero check is not required by the tests, but the cosine of an angle with a directionless vector is genuinely undefined, so raising beats returning a made-up number.
solutions.trap: Calling normalise where you meant magnitude gives you an array where a scalar belongs — then `if array == 0` raises “the truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous”.

solutions.name: most_similar
solutions.headline: search, and the version you have not written yet
solutions.mechanism: Short, because exercise 6 did the work. Iterating a dict yields its keys, and key= changes what gets compared, not what gets returned — so the comparison runs over scores while the return value is a name.
solutions.why: This is the definition, not the implementation. Stacking the library into a matrix and running L @ q scores everything in a single call — identical arithmetic, one operation instead of n. That is what a vector database actually runs over millions of rows, and it is what stretch.py asks for.
solutions.trap: max(scores.values()) hands you 0.998 with no way back to which item earned it.
